title: Neutropenic Sepsis
summary: Suspected infection in a patient at risk of neutropenia (e.g. chemotherapy within 6 weeks) — empiric IV antibiotics within 1 hour; do not wait for the neutrophil count.

sources.label: NICE CG151 — Neutropenic sepsis: prevention and management
NICE NG51 — Sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management

blocks.title: Treat as neutropenic sepsis if
blocks.body: Anticancer treatment (usually within the last 6 weeks) AND temperature ≥38 °C or any signs/symptoms of significant sepsis — even if afebrile. Give empiric antibiotics FIRST; never wait for the FBC result.

items: ABCDE; full set of observations and early warning score
Ask about chemotherapy regimen, last cycle date, indwelling lines (PICC/Hickman), recent transfusions and prophylaxis
Examine for a source, including line sites, perineum (no PR examination in neutropenia), mouth, skin, chest, urine
Bloods: FBC, U&E, LFT, CRP, lactate, coagulation; blood cultures (peripheral AND from each lumen of any central line) before antibiotics if this causes no delay
Cultures/swabs from any suspicious site; CXR if respiratory features
Give high-flow oxygen if needed to keep SpO₂ in target range
Take blood cultures (do not delay antibiotics beyond 1 hour)
Give empiric IV broad-spectrum antibiotics per local policy — commonly piperacillin/tazobactam 4.5 g IV (check allergy status; verify choice and dose against local policy)
Start IV fluid resuscitation if hypotensive or lactate raised
Monitor urine output; consider catheter if shocked

rows: Escalate — this is a breach; give immediately
Fluid bolus, senior review, consider critical care
Confirms neutropenia — continue pathway, involve oncology/haematology

blocks.title: Pearl
blocks.body: Neutropenic patients may not mount fever, pus, or an impressive CRP. A chemotherapy patient who 'just feels awful', is hypothermic, or has unexplained hypotension deserves the same 1-hour pathway as the febrile one.

blocks.title: Why the 1-hour target?
blocks.body: In neutropenia the usual host barriers to bacteraemia are absent, so gram-negative sepsis can progress to shock over hours. Empiric anti-pseudomonal cover given within the first hour is the single intervention most consistently associated with reduced mortality, which is why the antibiotic decision is made on risk (recent chemotherapy + illness), not on a confirmed neutrophil count.
